semantic_correction.stem: A client receiving maintenance hemodialysis has a functioning arteriovenous fistula in the left forearm. The right arm is available for routine measurements. The RN sees assistive personnel preparing to place a blood-pressure cuff on the left arm. Which action is most appropriate?

options.A: Allow the blood-pressure measurement on the fistula arm because the cuff will be inflated for only a brief period of time.
options.B: Stop the measurement and use the other arm, protecting the fistula arm from blood-pressure cuffs and routine venipuncture.
options.C: Place the cuff above the fistula instead of over it, because pressure proximal to the access will not affect fistula blood flow.
options.D: Use the fistula arm for blood pressure but avoid venipuncture there, because needle puncture is the main threat to the access.

semantic_correction.rationale: The 2026 NCSBN NCLEX-RN Test Plan explicitly includes managing the care of clients receiving hemodialysis under Physiological Adaptation. Current National Kidney Foundation vascular-access guidance instructs patients and healthcare teams to protect a hemodialysis fistula or graft by avoiding blood-pressure cuffs and blood draws on the access arm; the other arm should be used when available. NIDDK likewise emphasizes preservation and protection of arm vessels for dialysis access. Because this client has a functioning left-arm fistula and the right arm is available, B is the uniquely best response. A permits unnecessary compression of the access arm. C still places cuff pressure on the access extremity and invents a safe location on the same arm. D incorrectly treats venipuncture as the only relevant threat while still exposing the access arm to cuff compression. Therefore B is correct.
semantic_correction.educational_objective: Protect a functioning hemodialysis AV fistula or graft by avoiding routine blood-pressure cuff compression and venipuncture on the access arm when another site is available.

near_duplicate_check.note: V2-Q0823 tests PD-associated peritonitis. V2-Q0622 tests malfunctioning equipment. V2-Q0724 tests acute deterioration escalation. V2-Q0824 tests protection of a functioning hemodialysis AV fistula from BP cuff/venipuncture. Targeted repository search returned no matching hemodialysis-access protection item before staging.

option_audit.A: Plausible because cuff use is brief, but access-arm compression is avoidable and contrary to vascular-access protection guidance.
option_audit.B: Correct. It protects the access arm and uses the available nonaccess arm.
option_audit.C: Plausible attempt to avoid direct fistula compression but still exposes the access extremity to cuff pressure and invents a safe same-arm position.
option_audit.D: Plausible partial access protection but incorrectly permits cuff compression and treats venipuncture as the sole risk.

ambiguity_check: No second defensible best answer. The other arm is explicitly available. B alone follows established access-protection guidance by avoiding both BP cuff use and routine venipuncture on the fistula arm.
